en.title: Ted Lasso's Latest Episode Tackles Cliques the 'Lasso Way'
en.summary: The beloved AFC Richmond team faces internal divisions as cliques form among the Lady Greyhounds. Ted Lasso's signature approach aims to unite the squad, but does it go deep enough?
en.body:
## The Greyhounds' Inner Circle

**Ted Lasso** has always excelled at finding the heart in unexpected places, and its latest episode turns its folksy charm towards a familiar pop culture trope: the clique. Drawing parallels to iconic teen dramas like **Mean Girls** and **Heathers**, the show explores how even professional athletes can fall into the trap of forming exclusive groups. The Lady Greyhounds, facing the pressures of competition, have fractured into distinct factions: the strategic midfielders, the defensive stalwarts, and the flashy attackers. This internal division threatens to undermine their team cohesion just as much as any opponent on the pitch.

The show’s approach to resolving this, however, is pure **Ted Lasso**. Instead of prolonged drama or simmering resentment, the issue is addressed with characteristic optimism and a touch of gentle intervention from Ted, Beard, and their colleagues. While this method aligns with the show's core ethos of kindness and understanding, the rapid resolution leaves some fans wondering if the underlying issues were explored with sufficient depth. The swiftness with which these newly formed cabals are dismantled, even involving a stint behind bars, feels somewhat rushed, especially considering the show's established track record with character development.

## Beyond the Surface Level

The narrative raises a pertinent question for fans: are these cliques merely a plot device, or do they represent a deeper exploration of the new players' psyches? The AV Club notes that the episode name-drops various pop culture cliques, suggesting an awareness of the trope. However, the article points out a potential pitfall: the show hasn't yet delved deeply into the motivations or backgrounds of these new characters. Unlike the richly developed arcs of **Jamie Tartt** or **Roy Kent** in earlier seasons, the current ensemble of Lady Greyhounds feels less fleshed out. We understand *that* cliques have formed, but the *why* and *how* of their formation, and the true nature of their conflicts, remain somewhat elusive. This leaves an opportunity for richer storytelling that could elevate these characters beyond archetypes.

## What's Next for AFC Richmond

As the season progresses, the success of **Ted Lasso** will hinge on its ability to balance its signature feel-good moments with meaningful character arcs for its expanding roster. The hope is that the show will dedicate more screen time to exploring the nuances of these new dynamics, allowing fans to connect with the entire team. Future episodes will likely show the long-term impact of this clique-busting mission and whether genuine bonds can truly overcome ingrained social divisions.

content_raw: Here’s a quick (non-pub) quiz for you: Are cliques considered inherently negative because pop culture tends to portray them as such? I’m talking the Plastics, the Heathers, the Chanels, you name it (as this Ted Lasso episode does, too, by name-dropping Mean Girls , Heathers , and even The Lost Boys ). These tight-knit crews are usually framed as women who tend to act superior to people not in their crew, and pick on or shut down outsiders who don’t conform to their made-up rules. These specific examples are from young adult stories, but if Ted Lasso ‘s latest episode wants to say anything, it’s that teen girls and professional athletes are somehow similar (because they’re driven by ego and how other perceive them), at least according to AFC Richmond’s former psychologist, who helpfully states that cliques can be a way for people to build a community in a stressful environment.  After establishing that the Lady Greyhounds have formed three distinct cliques—the logical midfielders, the protective but anxious defenders, the exciting but selfish attackers—the show approaches this in, what else, the Lasso Way. That is, it’s all handled in an appropriately “aw shucks!” manner within a still-too-long 45-minute episode. We’re introduced to these cabals just as swiftly as they’re broken up by Ted, Beard, Alice, and a stint behind bars. The whole thing feels sweet, sure, but rushed, because Ted Lasso still hasn’t gone deep with any of its new players—at least not like they did with Jamie Tartt or Roy Kent in season one. We don’t exactly know why these mini teams were formed in the first place, how they managed to function well on the field despite it, and what their beef truly was (except for some lame jabs exchanged during Ted’s speech).  If we haven’t seen these women play or fight properly—barring one dust-up that Ted and Beard barge in to interrupt after covering their eyes—how are we to care about the method in which their differences are resolved? Luckily, Ted Lasso can apply one of its greatest strengths here: performers whose charm can overcome any hamfisted script. Jason Sudeikis and Tanya Reynolds sell the hell out of Ted and Alice’s budding banter, and even Brendan Hunt has mercifully toned down Beard’s weirdness a little bit. Meanwhile, the Lady Greyhounds are making the most of their weirdly limited screentime. So when the episode ends with all of them chanting together as they walk out of jail, it is effective—and for now, I’ll take that as a win.  “Greyhounds’ Day Off” treads familiar ground with the whole clique thing and the back-and-forth between Roy and Keeley. Look, Juno Temple and Brett Goldstein ooze chemistry, it’s undeniable, but I’m over the show finding ridiculous ways to keep them apart.
